newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African court convicts policeman-turned-activist.
newsitem.headline: S.African court convicts policeman-turned-activist.

text.p: A South African court on Thursday convicted a white former policeman and two black accomplices of the brutal 1981 murder of prominent anti-apartheid lawyer Griffiths Mxenge.

The court found Dirk Coetzee, former commander of a covert police assassination squad who later joined President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC), and former policemen Almond Nofomela and David Tshikalanga guilty of stabbing Mxenge to death in a deserted sports stadium.
Mxenge represented many ANC members while the organisation was banned under apartheid laws.

Coetzee was the first white policeman involved in covert operations against the ANC to turn on the apartheid system and publicly reveal details of the state campaign against Mandela's liberation army.
The three former policemen are among more than 6,000 South Africans who have applied for amnesty under a National Unity and Reconciliation Act designed to heal the wounds of apartheid.
A decision on their applications could be expected in mid-June, Coetzee's lawyer Julian Knight said.
The murder trial was postponed to July 1, to give the defence teams time to prepare their arguments for mitigation.

Passing judgment in the east coast port city of Durban, Judge Piet Combrinck told the packed court that confessions made by the three men to a 1990 commission probing police hit-squads could be used against them.
He said the failure of the accused to take the stand to refute their confessions meant that they had told the truth about their involvement in killing Mxenge.

"The accused in this matter have spurned the opportunity of telling us that their confessions were false. They must bear the consequences. The only reasonable inference to draw from their failure to testify is that their confessions are genuine."
Two other defendants, Andy Taylor and Johannes van der Hoven, both former senior Durban security branch policemen, were acquitted of the same charges.
Coetzee told reporters the judgment had not come as a surprise to him:

"It would have been a hell of a surprise if we were found not guilty. But I am not feeling desperate, there are enough backstops which include our amnesty applications and appeals to the constitutional court."
Mxenge's son, Mbasa, who was 15 at the time of the murder, wrote in the weekly Sunday Times that he could never forgive his fahter's killers.

"I understand and support the political need for reconciliation. Intellectually I grasp the importance of amnesty. But somewhere between the needs of the country and my deep personal sense of loss and anger, in my heart I cannot forgive," he said.
Mxenge's brother Mava told reporters outside the court the family was delighted with the judgment and called for life sentences to be handed down.
